Reproducing Kussovska, Kim and Rungratsameetaweemana (2025) from dandiset 000469¶

Paper. Kussovska D, Kim R, Rungratsameetaweemana N (2025). Neural heterogeneity shapes the temporal structure of human working memory. bioRxiv, doi:10.1101/2025.10.31.684900. The claims file (claims/kussovska-2025.yaml) was written from the bioRxiv full text posted on 1 November 2025 (main text, figure legends and Methods; the Extended Data figures and their legends were not in the text read).

Dandiset. DANDI:000469, version 0.231213.2047 (Kyzar et al. 2024, human single neurons during a Sternberg working memory task). This is the version the paper cites (Methods, Participants and data source, and Data availability). The four published versions (0.231213.2047, 0.240122.1800, 0.240122.1812, 0.240123.1806) hold the same 41 assets with the same asset identifiers and sizes, which the data check below confirms, so the version the paper's code downloads (0.240123.1806) gives the same data.

Paper's code. github.com/dariakussovska/heterogeneitywm at commit 5144fe8, the commit the claims file read. Four of its shipped tables are outside inputs here: data/new_trial_info.xlsx (the 96 load-matched trials of the GLM), data/new_trial_final.xlsx (the 75 identity-matched trials of the pseudo-population decoding), both of which the claims file names as readings, and, for comparison only (no outcome rests on them), data/all_neuron_brain_regions_cleaned.xlsx (the code's concept-cell list) and data/cell_analysis/Cell_metrics.xlsx (the code's ACG features). The rodent validation claim uses data/cell_analysis/validation_data.xlsx, the features of the CellExplorer ground-truth cells (data: elsewhere).

BY = {s["sub"]: s for s in sessions}
NT = wm.neuron_table(sessions)
T = {s["sub"]: wm.trial_frame(s) for s in sessions}

The pinned version holds 41 files, a screening session (ses-1) and a Sternberg session (ses-2) for each of 21 subjects except sub-19, which has only ses-2: 41 sessions from 21 patients, as the paper says. Every published version holds the same assets. The analysis reads only the 21 Sternberg files, as the paper's code does.

The files hold 902 units (as the paper says) in five regions, each with a left and a right label. Fifteen sessions have 135 trials and six have 108 (subjects 6, 7, 8, 9, 16 and 19); the paper says sixteen and five, so the data disagree with the description there. The ages run from 17 to 70 (mean 36.19); the paper gives 17 to 71 and 36.10 over sessions, which one Sternberg file per subject cannot check.

Every session has equal numbers of trials per load and five images (ids 1 to 5) in its encoding periods. The epoch timestamps are ordered in every trial except one: in subject 9 (the session marked False above) one trial has a maintenance timestamp equal to its probe timestamp, a maintenance of 0 s (trial 29, load 1), and another (trial 89) has a fixation of 31 us. Apart from that trial, maintenance lasts about 2.53 to 2.84 s (paper: 2.5 to 2.8 s). Fixation lasts about 0.91 to 1.2 s in most sessions, longer than the paper's 0.9 to 1.0 s, with single long fixations (14.07 s in subject 21). The first encoding image lasts 1.0, 1.2, 1.5 or 2.5 s depending on the session (enc1_s); the paper does not state the image duration, and the code's 1 s encoding window is used throughout. No neuron of subject 9 fires in that fixation, and leaving it out changes the fixation statistics by at most the amounts printed. The 0 s trial is kept, as in the code: it adds an empty trial to the burst trains of the 2.8 s and 3 s windows and none to the own-maintenance reading, and its 2.5 s maintenance window in the decoding analyses holds the probe period. Spike times are in seconds and span each session's trials; the contrast below checks the clock.

In [5]:
# Clock check by contrast: image selectivity of each neuron 200 to 1000 ms after the first
# encoding onset (the concept-cell window) against the same test in windows shifted 1 s and 2 s
# earlier (fixation and the previous trial's probe), per session. With aligned clocks only the
# true window should hold image information beyond the false-positive rate.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rows = []
for sub, t in T.items():
    nids = NT.nid[NT["sub"] == sub].values
    row = {"sub": sub, "neurons": len(nids)}
    for shift in [0.0, -1.0, -2.0]:
        k = 0
        for n in nids:
            r = wm.count_in(SPK[n], (t.enc1 + 0.2 + shift).values, (t.enc1 + 1.0 + shift).values) / 0.8
            k += wm.concept_test(r, t.img1.values, rng, reading="code")[2]
        row[f"selective_at_{shift:+.0f}s"] = k
    # evoked response: population rate 0-300 ms after onset over the 300 ms before
    pre = sum(wm.count_in(SPK[n], (t.enc1 - 0.3).values, t.enc1.values).sum() for n in nids)
    post = sum(wm.count_in(SPK[n], (t.enc1 + 0.2).values, (t.enc1 + 0.5).values).sum() for n in nids)
    row["rate_200_500ms_over_pre"] = round(post / max(pre, 1), 2)
    rows.append(row)
clk = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(clk.to_string(index=False))
print("totals:", clk[[c for c in clk.columns if c.startswith("selective")]].sum().to_dict())

Over all sessions, 58 neurons are image-selective in the window after the first encoding onset, against 11 and 16 in the windows shifted 1 s and 2 s earlier, so image information appears where the trials table puts the images. This is consistent with spike times and trials sharing a clock; it is shown per session only where selective neurons exist. Subjects 1, 3, 6, 10, 17, 19 and 20 have no selective neuron in the true window, and the population rate barely changes after image onset in any session (ratios 0.89 to 1.14), so for those seven sessions the alignment could not be established.

# Duplicate recordings: identical spike trains or identical trial tables across sessions.
keys = {}
dups = []
for n in range(len(NT)):
    s = SPK[n]
    k = (len(s), round(float(s[:5].sum()), 6) if len(s) else 0.0)
    if k in keys and NT["sub"].iat[keys[k]] != NT["sub"].iat[n]:
        dups.append((keys[k], n))
    keys.setdefault(k, n)
print("units with an identical spike train in another session:", len(dups))
tabs = {}
for sub, t in T.items():
    key = tuple(np.round(t.enc1.values[:10] - t.enc1.values[0], 4))
    tabs.setdefault(key, []).append(sub)
print("sessions with identical trial timing:", [v for v in tabs.values() if len(v) > 1])
seqs = {}
for sub, t in T.items():
    seqs.setdefault(tuple(t.img1.values) + tuple(t.load.values), []).append(sub)
print("sessions sharing the same trial sequence (loads and image ids):", [v for v in seqs.values() if len(v) > 1])

No unit or trial timing is duplicated across sessions. Several sessions share one trial sequence (the same loads and image ids in the same order), which is expected if the task used a fixed pseudorandom list; their timings differ, so these are separate recordings.

The code's tables match the dataset trial by trial: trial_id is the row of the trials table, and loads and reaction times agree exactly. In the identity-matched table the image index of every load-1 row is the same in all 21 sessions and maps one to one onto each session's picture ids, so its rows can align a pseudo-population; its load-2 and load-3 rows are aligned on the label image (second and third) in every session too. The code's neuron table lists the dataset's units in order, with the same locations. Several sessions share one trial sequence, and the subjects with 108 trials have 106 rows in new_trial_info.

rt-in-vs-out-memory¶

Reaction time was faster for probes held in memory than for probes not in memory.

In [12]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)


def paired_signflip(d, rng, n=1000):
    d = np.asarray(d)
    null = np.abs((rng.choice([-1, 1], (n, len(d))) * d).mean(1))
    return float((np.sum(null >= abs(d.mean())) + 1) / (n + 1))


def label_perm(x, lab, rng, n=1000):
    obs = x[lab].mean() - x[~lab].mean()
    null = np.array([(lambda p: x[p].mean() - x[~p].mean())(rng.permutation(lab)) for _ in range(n)])
    return obs, float((np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)) + 1) / (n + 1))


for name, sel in [("correct trials", tr.correct == 1), ("all trials", tr.correct >= 0)]:
    x = tr[sel]
    d = x.groupby(["sub", "in_memory"]).rt.median().unstack()
    diff = d[1] - d[0]
    pa = paired_signflip(diff.values, rng)
    obs, pb = label_perm(x.rt.values, x.in_memory.values == 1, rng)
    print(f"{name}: (a) median RT in memory {d[1].median():.3f} s, not in memory {d[0].median():.3f} s; "
          f"per-participant difference mean {diff.mean():.3f} s, faster in {(diff < 0).sum()} of {len(diff)}; sign-flip p = {pa:.4f}")
    print(f"   (b) pooled mean difference in - out = {obs:.3f} s, label permutation p = {pb:.4f}")
print("paper: permutation test P = 0.001")

fig1e-load-modulated-neurons¶

During maintenance a significant proportion of neurons in the preSMA (19.6%), vmPFC (18.75%) and dACC (10.53%) was modulated by memory load.

Spike counts in the first 2.5 s of maintenance, a Poisson GLM on the z-scored predictor fitted by Newton's method (the same maximum-likelihood fit as the code's unpenalised PoissonRegressor; checked against sklearn below), 1,000 permutations with seed 17. Trial readings: (a) the code's 96 load-matched trials (new_trial_info.xlsx: subject 1's new_trial_ids, each neuron's count from its own session's trial with the same id), with the permutation shared over the trial vector (the code) or drawn within each participant (Methods); (b) all trials of each participant, permuted within participant.

In [14]:
REG = {g: NT.nid[NT.region == g].values for g in ["AMY", "HPC", "dACC", "preSMA", "vmPFC"]}
NP = 1000


def glm_design(pred, trials, perm, seed=17):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    shared = np.array([rng.permutation(len(ids1)) for _ in range(NP)])
    subperm, Y, X, P = {}, [], [], []
    for n in range(len(NT)):
        sub = NT["sub"].iat[n]
        t = T[sub].set_index("trial")
        if trials == "matched":
            rows = INFO[INFO.subject_id == sub].set_index("new_trial_id").loc[ids1, "trial_id"].values
        else:
            rows = t.index.values
        tt = t.loc[rows]
        Y.append(wm.count_in(SPK[n], tt.maint.values, tt.maint.values + 2.5))
        if pred == "rt_code":
            X.append(INFO[INFO.subject_id == 1].set_index("new_trial_id").loc[ids1, "RT"].values)
        else:
            X.append(tt["load" if pred == "load" else "rt"].values)
        if perm == "shared":
            P.append(shared)
        else:
            if sub not in subperm:
                subperm[sub] = np.array([rng.permutation(len(rows)) for _ in range(NP)])
            P.append(subperm[sub])
    return Y, X, P


GLM = {}
for pred in ["load", "rt", "rt_code"]:
    for trials, perm in [("matched", "shared"), ("matched", "within"), ("all", "within")]:
        if pred == "rt_code" and trials == "all":
            continue
        Y, X, P = glm_design(pred, trials, perm)
        GLM[(pred, trials, perm)] = (wm.glm_fit(Y, X, P), Y, X)

# check of the fit against sklearn on 20 neurons
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor
(real, null), Y, X = GLM[("load", "matched", "shared")]
dev = []
for n in range(0, 902, 45):
    x = (X[n] - X[n].mean()) / X[n].std()
    if Y[n].sum() > 0:
        dev.append(abs(PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000).fit(x[:, None], Y[n]).coef_[0] - real[n]))
print(f"largest |slope - sklearn slope| over {len(dev)} neurons: {max(dev):.2e}")
print("neurons with no maintenance spikes in the matched trials:", int(sum(y.sum() == 0 for y in Y)))
for key in [("load", "matched", "shared"), ("load", "matched", "within"), ("load", "all", "within")]:
    (real, null), _, _ = GLM[key]
    df, _ = wm.glm_groups(real, null, REG)
    print(f"\nload, trials {key[1]}, permutation {key[2]}:")
    print(df.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("\npaper: preSMA 19.6% (P = 0.001), vmPFC 18.75% (P = 0.009), dACC 10.53% (P = 0.026); tolerance 10% of each")

In [15]:
# Stability check. The slope depends on the data only through sum(x * y), so a permutation of the
# three load levels often gives exactly the real slope, and a neuron can sit on its own threshold.
# The comparison '>=' is then decided by floating-point rounding, which can differ between machines
# and runs. 'raw' (above) compares the floats as the code does; 'in' counts values within a relative
# 1e-9 of the threshold as at it (the code's rule in exact arithmetic), 'out' as below it.
for key in [("load", "matched", "shared"), ("load", "matched", "within"), ("load", "all", "within"),
            ("rt", "matched", "shared"), ("rt", "all", "within")]:
    (real, null), _, _ = GLM[key]
    thr = np.quantile(np.abs(null), 0.95, axis=1, method="higher")
    at = np.abs(np.abs(real) - thr) <= 1e-9 * thr
    print(f"\n{key[0]}, trials {key[1]}, permutation {key[2]}: {int(at.sum())} neurons have |b1| within a relative 1e-9 "
          f"of their threshold {NT.region[at].value_counts().to_dict()}")
    tab = {ties: wm.glm_groups(real, null, REG, ties=ties)[0].set_index("group") for ties in ["raw", "in", "out"]}
    print(pd.DataFrame({f"{ties}_{c}": tab[ties][c] for ties in tab for c in ["significant", "percent", "p"]}).round(3).to_string())

Result: reproduced. Under reading (a) with the code's shared permutation, preSMA (20.40%, 51 of 250, p = 0.000), vmPFC (18.75%, p = 0.009) and dACC (10.53%, p = 0.025) are each within tolerance with p < 0.05; the within-participant permutation gives 19.20%, 18.75% and 9.94%, also within tolerance. With all trials (reading b) the three regions stay significant with higher percentages (22.80%, 21.88%, 12.87%). The amygdala and hippocampus are not significant under any reading. The stability check shows why these counts moved between runs: with load as the predictor 8 neurons (4 in preSMA) have |b1| equal to their own null threshold up to rounding, so the counts depend on the last bits of the fit. Counting those ties as significant (in) or not (out), the shared permutation gives preSMA 51 or 47 neurons (20.40% or 18.80%) and vmPFC 21.88% or 18.75%, so vmPFC leaves the tolerance when ties count; the within-participant permutation stays within tolerance for all three regions under every tie rule (preSMA 18.80 to 19.20%, vmPFC 18.75%, dACC 9.94%, p at most 0.029). The outcome does not depend on the rounding. With reaction time as the predictor no neuron sits on its threshold, and the counts do not change.

With each trial's own reaction time, the claim's test finds regions with a significant proportion of RT-modulated neurons after BH correction (preSMA, the amygdala and dACC under reading (a); see the p_BH column), and the percentages are higher than the paper's. The code's predictor, subject 1's RT vector applied to every neuron, gives the paper's three percentages exactly (AMY 5.79%, preSMA 8.00%, vmPFC 6.25%) and no region significant after correction under the shared permutation, so the paper's numbers come from that predictor, which pairs each neuron's counts with another participant's reaction times.

fig2ab-single-cells-not-persistent¶

Examined neuron by neuron, most concept cells did not maintain elevated firing for their preferred image throughout the maintenance epoch.

Per concept cell, load 1 trials, 50 ms bins of the first 2.5 s of maintenance, z-scored to fixation and smoothed (sigma one bin); preferred trials are those whose first image is the cell's preferred image. Reading (a): a permutation test per bin (1,000 shuffles of the preferred/nonpreferred labels), persistent when significantly higher on preferred trials in at least half the bins; reading (b): persistent when the spike count is significantly higher on preferred trials in each of the 1 s windows M1 to M3 (M3 ends at the end of maintenance).

CELLS_C = np.where(CONCEPT)[0]


def pref_mask(t, pref, load):
    if load == 1:
        return (t.img1 == pref).values
    return ((t.img1 == pref) | (t.img2 == pref) | (t.img3 == pref)).values


rows = []
for n in CELLS_C:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(int(n))
    t = T[NT["sub"].iat[n]]
    t = t[t.load == 1]
    pm = pref_mask(t, PREF[n], 1)
    Z = wm.psth_z(SPK[n], t.maint.values, 2.5, *FIX[n])
    obs = Z[pm].mean(0) - Z[~pm].mean(0)
    perms = [rng.permutation(pm) for _ in range(1000)]
    null = np.array([Z[q].mean(0) - Z[~q].mean(0) for q in perms])
    p = np.mean(np.abs(null) >= np.abs(obs), 0)
    frac = np.mean((p < 0.05) & (obs > 0))
    win = []
    for i in range(3):
        c = wm.count_in(SPK[n], t.maint.values + i, np.minimum(t.maint.values + i + 1, t.probe.values))
        o = c[pm].mean() - c[~pm].mean()
        nn = np.array([c[q].mean() - c[~q].mean() for q in perms])
        win.append(bool(o > 0 and np.mean(np.abs(nn) >= abs(o)) < 0.05))
    rows.append({"nid": n, "sub": NT["sub"].iat[n], "region": NT.region.iat[n], "pref_trials": int(pm.sum()),
                 "frac_bins_higher": frac, "M1": win[0], "M2": win[1], "M3": win[2]})
sc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
sc["persistent_a"] = sc.frac_bins_higher >= 0.5
sc["persistent_b"] = sc[["M1", "M2", "M3"]].all(1)

print(f"persistent under (b): {sc.persistent_b.sum()}; not persistent: {(~sc.persistent_b).sum()}")

print("by participant (persistent a / cells):", sc.groupby("sub").agg(cells=("nid", "size"), pa=("persistent_a", "sum"), pb=("persistent_b", "sum")).T.to_dict())

    print(f"threshold variant, persistent when at least {thr:.0%} of bins are higher: {(sc.frac_bins_higher >= thr).sum()} of {len(sc)}")

fig2c-population-persistence¶

Averaged across the 58 concept cells, firing on preferred trials stayed higher than on nonpreferred trials across the maintenance epoch of load 1 trials, a pattern of persistent activity.

Per cell the trial-mean z-scored, smoothed rate (50 ms bins) on preferred and nonpreferred trials, in the first encoding second, the first 2.5 s of maintenance and the first second of the probe (the three panels); per bin a bootstrap over cells (1,000, seed 42) of the mean preferred minus nonpreferred difference, two-sided, BH over all bins of all panels (per-panel BH as a variant). Readings: (a) significant bins cover at least half the maintenance bins; (b) every 500 ms segment holds a significant bin.

In [19]:
def population_persistence(load, seed=42):
    D = {"enc": [], "maint": [], "probe": []}
    for n in CELLS_C:
        t = T[NT["sub"].iat[n]]
        t = t[t.load == load]
        pm = pref_mask(t, PREF[n], load)
        for ep, on, dur in [("enc", t.enc1.values, 1.0), ("maint", t.maint.values, 2.5), ("probe", t.probe.values, 1.0)]:
            Z = wm.psth_z(SPK[n], on, dur, *FIX[n])
            D[ep].append(np.c_[Z[pm].mean(0), Z[~pm].mean(0)])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(CELLS_C), (1000, len(CELLS_C)))
    out = {}
    for ep, arr in D.items():
        a = np.array(arr)  # cells x bins x (pref, nonpref)
        d = a[:, :, 0] - a[:, :, 1]
        b = d[idx].mean(1)
        p = np.minimum(1, 2 * np.minimum(np.mean(b <= 0, 0), np.mean(b >= 0, 0)))
        out[ep] = (a.mean(0), d.mean(0), p)
    allp = np.concatenate([out[e][2] for e in ["enc", "maint", "probe"]])
    q = wm.bh(allp)
    nb = {e: len(out[e][2]) for e in out}
    qm = q[nb["enc"]:nb["enc"] + nb["maint"]]
    sig = (qm < 0.05) & (out["maint"][1] > 0)
    sig_panel = (wm.bh(out["maint"][2]) < 0.05) & (out["maint"][1] > 0)
    return out, sig, sig_panel


PERSIST = {}
for load in [1, 2, 3]:
    out, sig, sigp = population_persistence(load)
    PERSIST[load] = (out, sig, sigp)
    seg = [bool(sig[i * 10:(i + 1) * 10].any()) for i in range(5)]
    m = out["maint"][0]
    print(f"load {load}: maintenance mean z preferred {m[:, 0].mean():.3f}, nonpreferred {m[:, 1].mean():.3f}; "
          f"preferred above nonpreferred in {np.mean(m[:, 0] > m[:, 1]):.2f} of bins; significant bins (BH all panels) "
          f"{sig.mean():.2f} (per-panel BH {sigp.mean():.2f}); 500 ms segments with a significant bin {seg}")
    print(f"   ranges: preferred {m[:, 0].min():.2f} to {m[:, 0].max():.2f}, nonpreferred {m[:, 1].min():.2f} to {m[:, 1].max():.2f}")
out = PERSIST[1][0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3), sharey=True)
for a, ep, dur in zip(ax, ["enc", "maint", "probe"], [1.0, 2.5, 1.0]):
    x = np.arange(len(out[ep][1])) * 0.05
    a.plot(x, out[ep][0][:, 0], label="preferred")
    a.plot(x, out[ep][0][:, 1], label="nonpreferred")
    a.set_title(f"{ep}, load 1")
    a.set_xlabel("s from onset")
ax[0].set_ylabel("z-scored rate")
ax[0].legend()
plt.show()

Result: reproduced. At load 1 the population's preferred trace (mean z 0.761) is above the nonpreferred one (-0.013) in every maintenance bin, and every bin is significant after BH, so both readings hold. No point of the plot falls outside its axes, whose ranges are printed.

fig2d-cross-temporal-localized¶

In load 1 trials, decoders trained at specific times of encoding or early maintenance classified the image above chance at other times, but cross-time generalization clusters were sparse and temporally localized, so the information was not stably held across maintenance.

A pseudo-population of the concept cells on the code's identity-matched trials (load-1 rows of new_trial_final.xlsx, 30 trials, 6 per image; labels the first image), spike counts in 250 ms windows stepped by 100 ms from first-encoding onset over 5 s (the code's duration for load 1), z-scored with fixation; a linear SVM trained at each bin and tested at every bin with LOOCV. Per pair a binomial test against 20%, one-sided (P(X >= k)) or two-sided, BH over the grid. Cluster rules: (i) the code's, contours of the significance mask longer than 13 points (skimage.measure.find_contours); (ii) the Methods', a cluster-duration null from 1,000 label shuffles, a cluster kept when its temporal extent (the longer side of its bounding box, in bins, a choice of this attempt) exceeds the 95th percentile of the largest extent per shuffled map.

In [21]:
from skimage import measure


def ct_design(nids, load, label):
    subs = sorted(set(NT["sub"].values[nids]))
    rows, _ = wm.pseudo_rows(T, subs, load, "code", FINAL)
    f14 = FINAL[(FINAL.subject_id == 14) & (FINAL.num_images_presented == load)].sort_values("trial_id_final")
    y = f14["stimulus_index_enc1" if label == "first" else f"stimulus_index_enc{load}"].values
    dur = {1: 5, 2: 6, 3: 7}[load]
    st = wm.window_starts(0.25, 0.1, dur)
    X = np.zeros((len(y), len(nids), len(st)))
    for j, n in enumerate(nids):
        sub = NT["sub"].iat[n]
        t = T[sub].set_index("trial").loc[rows[sub]]
        X[:, j, :] = wm.zcounts(SPK[n], t.enc1.values, st, 0.25, *FIX[n])
    # epoch edges relative to first-encoding onset, mean over the participants' trials used
    rel = np.mean([(T[s].set_index("trial").loc[rows[s]].maint - T[s].set_index("trial").loc[rows[s]].enc1).mean() for s in subs])
    return X, y, st, rel


TWO_SIDED = {}


def sig_mask(acc, N, side):
    k = np.round(acc * N).astype(int)
    if side == "one":
        p = binom.sf(k - 1, N, 0.2)
    else:
        p = TWO_SIDED.setdefault(N, np.array([binomtest(kk, N, 0.2).pvalue for kk in range(N + 1)]))[k]
    q = wm.bh(p.ravel()).reshape(p.shape)
    return (q < 0.05) & (acc > 0.2)


def clusters(mask):
    lab, n = ndimage.label(mask)
    out = []
    for i, sl in enumerate(ndimage.find_objects(lab)):
        ext = max(sl[0].stop - sl[0].start, sl[1].stop - sl[1].start)
        out.append((i + 1, ext))
    return lab, out


def code_rule(mask):
    keep = np.zeros_like(mask)
    for c in measure.find_contours(mask.astype(float), 0.5):
        if len(c) > 13:
            r0, r1 = int(np.floor(c[:, 0].min())), int(np.ceil(c[:, 0].max()))
            c0, c1 = int(np.floor(c[:, 1].min())), int(np.ceil(c[:, 1].max()))
            keep[r0:r1 + 1, c0:c1 + 1] |= mask[r0:r1 + 1, c0:c1 + 1]
    return keep


def ct_analysis(nids, load, label, n_perm=1000, seed=0):
    X, y, st, rel = ct_design(nids, load, label)
    acc = wm.loo_cross_temporal(X, y)
    seeds = [wm.stable_seed("ct", load, label, len(nids), seed, i) for i in range(n_perm)]
    chunks = [seeds[i::4] for i in range(4)]
    perm_maps = sum(wm.pmap(wm.ct_perm_maps, [(X, y, c) for c in chunks]), [])
    res = {"acc": acc, "st": st, "rel": rel, "N": len(y)}
    for side in ["one", "two"]:
        m = sig_mask(acc, len(y), side)
        null_ext, null_sig = [], []
        for pm in perm_maps:
            pmask = sig_mask(pm, len(y), side)
            _, cl = clusters(pmask)
            null_ext.append(max([e for _, e in cl], default=0))
            null_sig.append(int(pmask.sum()))
        thr = np.percentile(null_ext, 95)
        lab, cl = clusters(m)
        keep_perm = np.isin(lab, [i for i, e in cl if e > thr])
        res[side] = {"mask": m, "null95": thr, "perm": keep_perm, "code": code_rule(m),
                     "null_ext_mean": float(np.mean(null_ext)), "obs_max_ext": max([e for _, e in cl], default=0),
                     "null_maps_with_sig": int(np.sum(np.array(null_sig) > 0)), "null_sig_max": int(max(null_sig)),
                     "n_perm": len(perm_maps)}
    return res


def summarize_ct(res, name):
    st, rel, acc = res["st"], res["rel"], res["acc"]
    enc_b = st + 0.25 <= rel
    mb = (st >= rel) & (st + 0.25 <= rel + 2.5)
    early = (st >= rel) & (st + 0.25 <= rel + 1.0)
    offdiag = ~np.eye(len(st), dtype=bool)
    rows = []
    for side in ["one", "two"]:
        for rule in ["code", "perm"]:
            k = res[side][rule]
            rows.append({"map": name, "binomial": side, "cluster_rule": rule,
                         "sig_pairs": int(res[side]["mask"].sum()), "kept_pairs": int(k.sum()),
                         "kept_offdiag": int((k & offdiag).sum()),
                         "train_bins_enc_or_early_with_offdiag": int(((k & offdiag)[enc_b | early]).any(1).sum()),
                         "max_frac_maint_test_bins_from_a_maint_train_bin": round(float(k[np.ix_(mb, mb)].mean(1).max()) if mb.any() else 0, 2),
                         "null95_extent": res[side]["null95"], "obs_largest_extent": res[side]["obs_max_ext"],
                         "shuffled_maps_with_sig_pairs": f"{res[side]['null_maps_with_sig']}/{res[side]['n_perm']}",
                         "most_sig_pairs_in_a_shuffled_map": res[side]["null_sig_max"]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


CT = {}
CT[("all", 1, "first")] = ct_analysis(CELLS_C, 1, "first")
r = CT[("all", 1, "first")]
print(f"{len(CELLS_C)} concept cells, {r['N']} trials, {len(r['st'])} bins; maintenance starts {r['rel']:.2f} s after first-encoding onset")
print(f"accuracy: diagonal mean {np.diag(r['acc']).mean():.3f}, range {r['acc'].min():.3f} to {r['acc'].max():.3f}; "
      f"mean largest cluster extent in shuffled maps {r['one']['null_ext_mean']:.1f} bins")

im = plt.imshow(r["acc"] * 100, origin="lower", vmin=0, vmax=100, cmap="viridis")
if r["one"]["code"].any():

Result: reproduced. Under every reading, 17 training bins in encoding or early maintenance have off-diagonal pairs kept above chance, and no maintenance training bin generalizes to more than 0.18 of the maintenance test bins, so the clusters are localized. Only 3 of the 1,000 shuffled maps have a significant pair after BH, one pair each, so the 95th percentile of their extent is 0, while the largest real cluster spans 26 bins; the rule as run cannot remove any real cluster. The one- and two-sided binomial tests keep the same pairs, as only accuracies above 20% are kept and both tests then reject at the same counts.

fig2e-maintenance-decoding-amy-mtl¶

Concept cells in the amygdala and in the MTL carried significant stimulus information during load 1 maintenance (35.56% and 32.13% decoding accuracy, chance 20%).

Within each participant, its concept cells in the region group, all its trials of the load, labels the last image; z-scored counts in 1 s windows stepped by 250 ms over the first 2.5 s of maintenance, concatenated; linear SVM, LOOCV; accuracy the mean over participants; p from 1,000 label shuffles, (k + 1) / 1001 on the mean over participants, BH within the load over the six region groups of the code (main_2e,supp_1f.py:14-21). Participants need at least three (Methods) or more than three (the code) concept cells in the group.

In [23]:
GROUPS_WP = {"AMY": ["AMY"], "HPC": ["HPC"], "dACC": ["dACC"], "preSMA": ["preSMA"],
             "MTL": ["AMY", "HPC"], "dACC_preSMA": ["dACC", "preSMA"]}
ST_WP = wm.window_starts(1.0, 0.25, 2.5)


def wp_design(g, sub, load):
    nids = NT[(NT["sub"] == sub) & NT.region.isin(GROUPS_WP[g]) & CONCEPT[NT.nid]].nid.values
    t = T[sub][T[sub].load == load]
    X = np.concatenate([wm.zcounts(SPK[n], t.maint.values, ST_WP, 1.0, *FIX[n]) for n in nids], 1)
    return X @ X.T, t["last"].values


units, designs = [], []
for g, regs in GROUPS_WP.items():
    for sub in sorted(T):
        k = int((CONCEPT & (NT["sub"] == sub).values & NT.region.isin(regs).values).sum())
        if k >= 3:
            for load in [1, 2, 3]:
                units.append((g, sub, load, k))
                designs.append(wp_design(g, sub, load))
nulls = wm.pmap(wm.perm_null_loo, [(K, y, 1000, wm.stable_seed("wp", g, s, L)) for (g, s, L, _), (K, y) in zip(units, designs)])
WP = pd.DataFrame([{"group": g, "sub": s, "load": L, "cells": k, "acc": wm.loo_correct(K, y).mean(), "trials": len(y), "null": nl}
                   for (g, s, L, k), (K, y), nl in zip(units, designs, nulls)])
print(WP[WP.load == 1][["group", "sub", "cells", "acc"]].assign(acc=lambda d: (100 * d.acc).round(2)).to_string(index=False))


def wp_stats(min_cells, load):
    rows = []
    for g in GROUPS_WP:
        x = WP[(WP.group == g) & (WP.load == load) & (WP.cells >= min_cells)]
        if len(x) == 0:
            continue
        m = x.acc.mean()
        nm = np.mean(np.stack(x.null.values), 0)
        # the paper's chance level of 20%: correct counts pooled over participants' trials, one-sided binomial
        k_tot = int(np.sum([a * n_ for a, n_ in zip(x.acc, x.trials)]).round())
        rows.append({"group": g, "participants": len(x), "accuracy_%": round(100 * m, 2),
                     "null_mean_%": round(100 * nm.mean(), 2), "p": (np.sum(nm >= m) + 1) / 1001,
                     "p_binom20": binomtest(k_tot, int(x.trials.sum()), 0.2, alternative="greater").pvalue})
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["p_BH"] = wm.bh(df.p)
    return df

    print(f"\nload 1, {name}:")
    print(wp_stats(mc, 1).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced. At load 1 the amygdala decodes at 35.63% and the MTL at 33.61% with at least three cells (p = 0.001 for both), and at 34.33% and 32.89% with more than three cells; all are within tolerance. Against the paper's 20% chance (one-sided binomial on the correct counts pooled over participants) p is below 1e-5 for all four (p_binom20). The label-shuffled nulls average about 17 to 18%, below 20%, as leave-one-out with shuffled labels is biased below chance; the p values against them are the code's.

fig2f-bin-width-decoding¶

In load 1 trials, pseudo-population decoding of the image during maintenance was above chance at every bin width and rose with bin width (250 ms 40.00%, 500 ms 56.67%, 750 ms 66.67%, 1000 ms 80.00%).

All concept cells, z-scored counts in windows of each width slid by 25 ms over the first 2.5 s of maintenance, concatenated; linear SVM, LOOCV; p from 1,000 label shuffles, (k + 1) / 1001; BH over the 12 tests of 4 widths and 3 loads. Trial readings: (a) the code's identity-matched rows (new_trial_final.xlsx), labels as the code takes them (subject 14's); (b) each participant's first six trials of each label image, aligned by image and rank. The fast SVM used here is checked against sklearn's SVC(kernel='linear').

In [25]:
WIDTHS = [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]


def bw_design(nids, load, reading, width):
    subs = sorted(set(NT["sub"].values[nids]))
    rows, lab = wm.pseudo_rows(T, subs, load, reading, FINAL)
    st = wm.window_starts(width, 0.025, 2.5)
    B = []
    for n in nids:
        sub = NT["sub"].iat[n]
        t = T[sub].set_index("trial").loc[rows[sub]]
        B.append(wm.zcounts(SPK[n], t.maint.values, st, width, *FIX[n]))
    return np.concatenate(B, 1), np.asarray(lab)


for reading in ["code", "rank"]:
    X, y = bw_design(CELLS_C, 1, reading, 1.0)
    print(f"reading {reading}: fast SVM equals sklearn SVC(kernel='linear') in every LOOCV prediction:",
          bool((wm.loo_correct(X @ X.T, y) == wm.loo_correct_sklearn(X, y)).all()))


def bw_run(name, nids):
    keys = [(reading, load, w) for reading in ["code", "rank"] for load in [1, 2, 3] for w in WIDTHS]
    des = [bw_design(nids, L, r, w) for r, L, w in keys]
    Ks = [X @ X.T for X, _ in des]
    nulls = wm.pmap(wm.perm_null_loo, [(K, y, 1000, wm.stable_seed("bw", name, *k)) for k, K, (_, y) in zip(keys, Ks, des)])
    res = {k: (wm.loo_correct(K, y), nl, X.shape) for k, K, (X, y), nl in zip(keys, Ks, des, nulls)}
    rows = []
    for (reading, load, w), (real, null, shape) in res.items():
        rows.append({"reading": reading, "load": load, "width_ms": int(w * 1000), "trials": shape[0], "features": shape[1],
                     "accuracy_%": round(100 * real.mean(), 2), "null_mean_%": round(100 * null.mean(), 2),
                     "p": (np.sum(null >= real.mean()) + 1) / 1001,
                     # the paper's chance level: one-sided binomial test of the correct count against 20%
                     "p_binom20": binomtest(int(real.sum()), len(real), 0.2, alternative="greater").pvalue})
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["p_BH"] = np.nan
    for reading in ["code", "rank"]:
        m = df.reading == reading
        df.loc[m, "p_BH"] = wm.bh(df.p[m])
    return res, df

# six load-1 trials per image in each participant (aligned by image and draw rank), 1000 ms width.
rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
subs = sorted(set(NT["sub"].values[CELLS_C]))
st = wm.window_starts(1.0, 0.025, 2.5)
accs = []
for d in range(20):
    rows = {}
    for s in subs:
        t = T[s][T[s].load == 1]
        rows[s] = np.concatenate([rng.permutation(t[t.img1 == im].trial.values)[:6] for im in range(1, 6)])
    B = []
    for n in CELLS_C:
        sub = NT["sub"].iat[n]
        t = T[sub].set_index("trial").loc[rows[sub]]
        B.append(wm.zcounts(SPK[n], t.maint.values, st, 1.0, *FIX[n]))
    Xr = np.concatenate(B, 1)
    accs.append(wm.loo_correct(Xr @ Xr.T, np.repeat(np.arange(1, 6), 6)).mean())
accs = 100 * np.array(accs)
print(f"random six-per-image draws, load 1, 1000 ms: accuracy median {np.median(accs):.1f}%, range {accs.min():.1f} to {accs.max():.1f}%")
real_code = 100 * BW["all"][0][("code", 1, 1.0)][0].mean()

Result: partially reproduced. Under both trial readings load-1 accuracy is above chance at every width (BH p at most 0.009) and rises from 250 to 1000 ms, but not every value is within tolerance: reading (a) gives 30.00, 60.00, 66.67 and 76.67% (250 ms below its tolerance of 36 to 44%), reading (b) 50.00, 66.67, 73.33 and 76.67% (250 and 500 ms above theirs). Random draws of six trials per image give 56.7 to 86.7% at 1000 ms, so the values depend on which trials enter, and this spread is wider than the tolerances. The label-shuffled nulls average 9 to 14%, below the paper's 20% chance. Against 20% (one-sided binomial, p_binom20) reading (a) at 250 ms (30.0%) has p = 0.13, so with the paper's chance level that value is not above chance; every other width and reading has p below 0.001.

fig2f-bin-width-pairwise¶

Pairwise, accuracy was higher for 750 than 250 ms, for 1000 than 250 ms and for 1000 than 500 ms bins, while 500 against 250, 1000 against 750 and 750 against 500 ms did not differ after correction.

Readings: (a) a paired permutation over trials swapping each trial's LOOCV correctness between the two widths (1,000), two-sided; (b) the observed difference against the differences of the two widths' shuffled nulls (paired by shuffle index), two-sided; BH over the six pairs.

import itertools
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
PAIRS = [(0.75, 0.25), (1.0, 0.25), (1.0, 0.5), (0.5, 0.25), (1.0, 0.75), (0.75, 0.5)]
for reading in ["code", "rank"]:
    res = BW["all"][0]
    rows = []
    for a, b in PAIRS:
        ca, na, _ = res[(reading, 1, a)]
        cb, nb, _ = res[(reading, 1, b)]
        obs = ca.mean() - cb.mean()
        sw = rng.random((1000, len(ca))) < 0.5
        nulla = (np.where(sw, cb, ca).mean(1) - np.where(sw, ca, cb).mean(1))
        pa = (np.sum(np.abs(nulla) >= abs(obs)) + 1) / 1001
        dn = na - nb
        pb = (np.sum(np.abs(dn - dn.mean()) >= abs(obs)) + 1) / 1001
        rows.append({"pair_ms": f"{int(a * 1000)} vs {int(b * 1000)}", "diff_%": round(100 * obs, 2), "p_a": pa, "p_b": pb})
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["p_a_BH"] = wm.bh(df.p_a)
    df["p_b_BH"] = wm.bh(df.p_b)
    print(f"trial reading {reading}:")
    print(df.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("paper: 750 vs 250 P = 0.026, 1000 vs 250 P = 0.004, 1000 vs 500 P = 0.032; the other three P > 0.05")

These three claims are tested in the second notebook of the entry, dpca_kussovska_2025.ipynb, which runs the 100 dPCA splits in parallel within the time limit.

acg-fit-yield¶

Fitting CellExplorer's triple-exponential model to each neuron's autocorrelogram and keeping well-fit units (R2 > 0.3) left 294 neurons for cell-type analysis.

A port of the code's MATLAB functions (calc_ACG_metrics.m, fit_ACG.m, Mean_ACG.m, normalize_acg_to_unit.m): narrow ACG (+/- 50 ms, 0.5 ms bins), the triple exponential fitted with CellExplorer's start point and bounds by bounded nonlinear least squares (scipy's trust-region reflective method in place of MATLAB's fit). Readings: (a) every spike of the unit; (b) only spikes within the trials (fixation onset to response).

In [29]:
FEAT = {}
for reading in ["a", "b"]:
    spikes = []
    for n in range(len(NT)):
        s = SPK[n]
        if reading == "b":
            t = T[NT["sub"].iat[n]]
            keep = np.zeros(len(s), bool)
            for a_, b_ in zip(t.fix_start.values, t.timestamps_Response.values):

                keep[i:j] = True
            s = s[keep]

    r = np.array(wm.pmap(wm.refit_acg, [(SPK[n], ss, ds) for n in range(len(NT))]))

Result: reproduced. 317 neurons have R2 > 0.3 under reading (a) and 298 under reading (b), both within tolerance. The firing rate and ISI CV of reading (a) equal the code's shipped table exactly, and the normalized mean ACG and Royer burst index agree within 1% for 99% of neurons, so the code used every spike of the unit. The fit itself is a limitation of this attempt: the fitted R2 agrees with the shipped MATLAB values within 1% for only 48% of neurons and the time constants for 7 to 11% (printed above), as scipy's optimizer finds other local optima than MATLAB's. Classification at R2 > 0.3 agrees for 97.5% of neurons, but tau_rise is a clustering feature, so the cell types of fig5c differ from the paper's, and tau_decay defines the decay groups of the burst analyses. The stability check shows that the fit is not stable at the level of rounding: changes of 1e-9 in the start point or 1e-12 in the ACG move R2 by more than 1e-3 for dozens of neurons and give 315 or 316 well-fit neurons against the main fit's 317 (the round-2 run of this notebook gave 316), with the reading (a) types of a few neurons changing. A run on another machine can therefore give any of these, and the cell-type counts and decay groups downstream move with them; the results that depend on them are checked under each variant (after ext2-bursts-loads23 and in fig6e).

def type_tests(F, types, cols):
    rows = []
    for c in cols:
        a, b = F[c][types == "IN"].dropna(), F[c][types == "PY"].dropna()
        u = mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided")
        rows.append({"feature": c, "IN_median": a.median(), "PY_median": b.median(), "U_IN_vs_PY": u.statistic, "p": u.pvalue})
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
    df["p_BY"] = multipletests(df.p, method="fdr_by")[1]
    return df


for reading in ["a", "b"]:
    df = type_tests(FEAT[reading], TYPES[reading], ["firing_rate", "acg_norm", "tau_rise", "burst_royer", "cv_isi"])
    print(f"reading ({reading}):")
    print(df.to_string(index=False))

fig5gh-burst-index-cv2¶

Putative pyramidal neurons had a higher burst index (0.985 against 0.622) and greater spike-train irregularity (CV2 1.673 against 1.319) than putative interneurons.

Result: reproduced. With the types and burst index of reading (b) and the CV of each unit's session interspike intervals (the column the code feeds to Fig. 5h), the medians are burst index PY 0.947 and IN 0.622 and CV PY 1.593 and IN 1.322, all within tolerance, PY higher on both with p below 0.005 (printed above). The group means of the burst index are far from the paper's (PY 5.6, a few very large values), so the paper's numbers match medians. Under reading (a) the PY burst-index median (0.802) is outside tolerance and its corrected p is 0.114. Holt's CV2 is lower than the paper's values (PY 1.18, IN 0.93).

supp4-rodent-validation (data elsewhere)¶

Applied to a labelled rodent dataset of 44 pyramidal neurons and 299 PV and SST interneurons, the spectral-clustering classifier assigned 333 of 343 neurons correctly (97%).

Tested on the features of the CellExplorer ground-truth cells that the paper's code ships (validation_data.xlsx), clustered as in fig5c, each cluster labelled by its majority type.

fig4c-encoding-bursts-vs-poisson¶

During encoding, population bursting did not exceed a rate-matched Poisson null for most neuronal groups; it differed from the null only for all neurons and for the low mean ACG amplitude group.

Within each participant and group, load 1 trials, the first encoding second; pooled spikes of the group, trials concatenated, 70 ms bins, Gaussian smoothing (sigma 40 ms), peaks at least 2 bins apart; 100 rate-matched Poisson surrogates; paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank over participants (the code's zero_method='pratt', asymptotic) and BH over the code's eight groups. Readings: peak rule (prominence, the code and Results; or height above the 90th percentile, the Methods), surrogate threshold (the real train's, the code; or each surrogate's own), group rule (the code's 6 lowest and highest; or the Methods' median split), all neurons (902 in participants with at least 10, or the well-fit neurons), and a 1-bin spacing variant.

def real_vs_null(df, groups=FAM, extra=("AllFit",)):
    out = []
    for g in list(groups) + list(extra):
        x = df[df.group == g]
        if len(x) < 2:
            continue
        w = wilcoxon(x.real, x.sur, zero_method="pratt", method="asymptotic")
        out.append({"group": g, "n": len(x), "real_median": x.real.median(), "null_median": round(x.sur.median(), 1),
                    "real_above": int((x.real > x.sur).sum()), "W": w.statistic, "p": w.pvalue})
    o = pd.DataFrame(out)
    m = o.group.isin(groups)
    o.loc[m, "p_BH"] = wm.bh(o.p[m])
    o.loc[~m, "p_BH"] = np.nan
    return o


def show_bursts(epoch, groups=FAM):
    summ = []
    for (grule, rule, dist, thr), df in BR[BR.epoch == epoch].groupby(["grule", "rule", "dist", "thr"]):
        o = real_vs_null(df, groups)
        o.insert(0, "reading", f"{grule}/{rule}/d{dist}/{thr}")
        summ.append(o)
    return pd.concat(summ)


BURST_ENC = show_bursts("enc")
print(BURST_ENC.round(4).to_string(index=False))

def fig4c_rule(o, all_name="All902"):
    sig = dict(zip(o.group, o.p_BH < 0.05))
    if all_name == "AllFit":
        sig["All902"] = bool(o[o.group == "AllFit"].p.iloc[0] < 0.05)
    named = sig["All902"] and sig["LowACG"]
    others = [g for g in ["HighACG", "ShortDecay", "LongDecay", "Concept"] if sig[g]]
    return named, others


for reading, o in BURST_ENC.groupby("reading", sort=False):
    for alln in ["All902", "AllFit"]:
        named, others = fig4c_rule(o, alln)
        print(f"{reading}, all neurons as {alln}: all and low ACG differ {named}; other groups that differ {others}")

Result: reproduced. Under the Methods' groups with the height rule and the real threshold, all neurons (BH p 0.0054) and the low ACG group differ from the Poisson null and the other four groups do not, both with the criterion's main spacing of 2 bins (low ACG BH p 0.0483, others 0.67 to 0.89) and with the 1-bin spacing of the Results' 70 ms, which the criterion runs as a variant (low ACG 0.0385, others 0.78 to 0.89). Under the code's groups with the prominence rule all neurons and low ACG differ but the concept group does too (BH p 0.045), the criterion's partial outcome. The Methods' groups with prominence make every group but concept cells differ; with the code's groups and the height rule the low ACG group does not differ. The reading this outcome rests on is the height rule, under which, in fig4-acg-group-differences, low ACG neurons burst less than high ACG neurons; the claims of Fig. 4 that hold under the prominence rule are not supported by the same rule as this one. How this result moves with the ACG fit is checked after ext2-bursts-loads23: with 2 bins one of the three rounding-level variants misses it (low ACG 0.0601), with 1 bin none does.

fig4d-maintenance-bursts-vs-poisson¶

During maintenance, bursting exceeded the Poisson null for all neurons pooled and for the low and high mean ACG and short and long tau decay groups, but not for concept cells.

# The criterion's own-maintenance reading under every reading: each trial's own maintenance (at
# most 2.8 s) concatenated with stride = its duration, surrogate spikes drawn within it.
BURST_MO = show_bursts("maint_own")
print(BURST_MO.round(4).to_string(index=False))


def fig4d_rule(o):
    ok = {g: bool((o[o.group == g].p_BH < 0.05).iloc[0] and (o[o.group == g].real_above > o[o.group == g].n / 2).iloc[0])
          for g in ["All902", "LowACG", "HighACG", "ShortDecay", "LongDecay"]}
    return ok, float(o[o.group == "Concept"].p_BH.iloc[0])


for reading, o in BURST_MO.groupby("reading", sort=False):
    ok, pc = fig4d_rule(o)
    print(f"own maintenance, {reading}: five named groups above the null {all(ok.values())} {ok}; concept cells corrected p {pc:.3f}")

# Control for the 2.8 s window: spike trains with no bursts. For each participant and group, every
# neuron's spikes are replaced by a homogeneous Poisson train within each trial's own maintenance
# (the trial's count as its mean), then tested as in the 2.8 s reading (surrogates spread over the
# whole 2.8 s) and as in the own-maintenance reading.
rows = []
for grule in ["code", "methods"]:
    for rule in ["prominence", "height"]:
        for g, subs in GR[grule].items():
            if g not in FAM:
                continue
            for sub, nids in subs.items():
                rng = np.random.default_rng(wm.stable_seed("control", grule, rule, g, sub))
                fake = [[np.sort(rng.uniform(0, d, rng.poisson(len(s)))) for s, d in zip(EP[(n, 1, "maint28")], MDUR[sub])] for n in nids]
                for win_reading, durs in [("2.8 s window", None), ("own maintenance", MDUR[sub])]:
                    rc, sc, _, _ = wm.group_bursts(fake, 2.8, rng, rule, 2, "real", durs=durs)
                    rows.append(dict(grule=grule, rule=rule, window=win_reading, group=g, sub=sub, real=rc, sur=sc))
CTRL = pd.DataFrame(rows)
for (grule, rule, wr), df in CTRL.groupby(["grule", "rule", "window"], sort=False):
    o = real_vs_null(df, FAM, ())
    print(f"\ncontrol (Poisson trains, no bursts), {grule}/{rule}/real, {wr}:")
    print(o[["group", "n", "real_median", "null_median", "real_above", "p", "p_BH"]].round(4).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced. The 2.8 s window of the code cannot decide this claim. Real spikes stop at the probe (2.53 to 2.84 s) while the surrogate spikes fill the whole 2.8 s, and the control above shows that this alone makes trains with no bursts exceed the null: Poisson trains confined to each trial's maintenance give all neurons above the null in 17 to 20 of 20 participants (BH p 0.0005 to 0.0025), and with the Methods' groups and the height rule all five named groups exceed it (BH p at most 0.016). With each trial's own maintenance the same control gives no group above the null (no BH p below 0.05 with more real than surrogate bursts). The outcome therefore rests on the own-maintenance reading of the criterion. Under it, the Methods' groups with the prominence rule give the paper's pattern with the real threshold (spacing 2 or 1 bin) and with each surrogate's own threshold: all five named groups exceed the null in most participants with BH p below 0.05, and concept cells do not (BH p 0.09 to 0.35). The code's groups and the height rule do not give it (high ACG or short tau decay fail). Under the 2.8 s window, for comparison, the real-threshold readings give the pattern too, which the control shows is expected without any bursts.

fig4-acg-group-differences¶

The low mean ACG group burst more than the high mean ACG group in both encoding and maintenance, whereas the short tau decay group exceeded the long tau decay group only during encoding.

Real burst counts of the two previous sections compared between groups within participant (paired two-sided Wilcoxon), BH over the code's 28 pairs of 8 groups, and over the four tests named here.

for (grule, rule, dist, thr), df in BR.groupby(["grule", "rule", "dist", "thr"]):
    if dist != 2 or thr != "real":
        continue
    res = {}
    for epoch in ["enc", "maint"]:
        x = df[df.epoch == epoch].pivot(index="sub", columns="group", values="real")
        pairs = list(itertools.combinations(FAM, 2))
        ps = {}
        for a, b in pairs:
            xx = x[[a, b]].dropna()
            try:
                ps[(a, b)] = wilcoxon(xx[b], xx[a], zero_method="wilcox").pvalue if len(xx) >= 2 else np.nan
            except ValueError:
                ps[(a, b)] = 1.0
        q28 = dict(zip(ps, wm.bh(np.nan_to_num(list(ps.values()), nan=1.0))))
        res[epoch] = (x, ps, q28)
    four = [("enc", "LowACG", "HighACG"), ("maint", "LowACG", "HighACG"), ("enc", "ShortDecay", "LongDecay"), ("maint", "ShortDecay", "LongDecay")]

              f"p = {p:.4f}, BH over 28 pairs {res[e][2][(a, b)]:.4f}, over these four {q:.4f}")

Result: partially reproduced. Under the prominence rule the low ACG group bursts more than the high ACG group in both epochs, in all 12 participants (p = 0.0005, BH p at most 0.0017), and short and long tau decay do not differ in maintenance; but short tau decay does not exceed long tau decay in encoding (p 0.14 with the code's groups, 0.086 with the Methods'). Under the height rule the low ACG group bursts less than the high ACG group. The tau decay groups come from this attempt's fit; groups built from the code's shipped tau decay are tested after ext2-bursts-loads23.

Burst detection of fig4c per epoch (encoding and probe 1 s, maintenance up to 3 s); M1 to M3 are (a) the Methods' 1 s windows from maintenance onset (peaks counted by their time in the trial; M3 runs from 2 s to the end of maintenance, 0.5 to 0.8 s), (b) the code's thirds of the whole concatenated train, or (c) the first, second and final thirds of each trial's own maintenance (peaks counted by their time in the trial), the reading of the Fig. 6c legend ("the first, second, and final thirds of the maintenance epoch"), which the claims file does not list and which is run here as a variant (M-trial; see questions/kussovska-2025.yaml). Paired two-sided Wilcoxon, BH over the 10 pairs of periods, per group and load.

PER = ["enc", "M1", "M2", "M3", "probe"]
rows = []
for grule, G in GR.items():
    for rule in ["prominence", "height"]:
        for mr in ["methods", "code", "trial"]:
            for L in [1, 2, 3]:
                for g, subs in G.items():
                    for sub, nids in subs.items():
                        c = wm.epoch_burst_counts({"enc": [EP[(n, L, "enc")] for n in nids],
                                                   "maint": [EP[(n, L, "maint3")] for n in nids],
                                                   "probe": [EP[(n, L, "probe")] for n in nids]}, rule, 2, mr,
                                                  mdurs=T[sub][T[sub].load == L].maint_dur.values)
                        rows.append(dict(grule=grule, rule=rule, mread=mr, load=L, group=g, sub=sub, **c))
EPB = pd.DataFrame(rows)


def epoch_tests(x):
    ps, names = [], []
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(PER, 2):
        try:
            p = wilcoxon(x[a], x[b], zero_method="wilcox").pvalue
        except ValueError:
            p = 1.0
        ps.append(p)
        names.append(f"{a}-{b}")
    q = wm.bh(ps)
    return dict(zip(names, q)), dict(zip(names, ps))


MD_L = {(s, L): t[t.load == L].maint_dur.mean() for s, t in T.items() for L in [1, 2, 3]}


def epoch_table(group, load):
    out = []
    for (grule, rule, mr), x in EPB[(EPB.group == group) & (EPB.load == load)].groupby(["grule", "rule", "mread"]):
        q, _ = epoch_tests(x)
        med = x[PER].median()
        # Under the Methods' windows M3 runs from 2 s to the end of maintenance (0.5 to 0.8 s), so
        # its count is also given per second; M1 and M2 last 1 s.
        m3_rate = np.median(x.M3.values / (np.array([MD_L[(s, load)] for s in x["sub"]]) - 2.0)) if mr == "methods" else np.nan
        out.append({"reading": f"{grule}/{rule}/M-{mr}", "n": len(x), **{f"med_{k}": med[k] for k in PER},
                    "med_M3_per_s": round(float(m3_rate), 2), **{f"q_{k}": round(q[f"enc-{k}"], 4) for k in PER[1:]},
                    "min_q_other": round(min(v for k, v in q.items() if not k.startswith("enc-")), 4),
                    "q_M1-M2": round(q["M1-M2"], 4), "q_M1-M3": round(q["M1-M3"], 4)})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


for g in ["All902", "AllFit"]:
    print(f"\n{g}, load 1 (medians are bursts per window; q is BH over the 10 pairs):")
    print(epoch_table(g, 1).to_string(index=False))

M3 under reading (a) lasts 0.67 s on average; its median rate per second, all neurons, prominence: 17.1 against M1 17.0

Result: partially reproduced. Under the prominence rule all 902 neurons burst more in each of M1, M2 and M3 than in encoding (medians 6 against 14 to 17, BH p 0.0003 to 0.035) under both window readings, but the probe does not differ from encoding under any reading (BH p 0.61 to 0.71; medians 6.0 and 5.5). Three of the four comparisons hold. Under the Methods' windows M3 runs from 2 s to the end of maintenance (0.67 s on average), so its count is low; per second its median is 16.6 (prominence) and 43.2 (height), against 17 and 46.5 in M1 (med_M3_per_s). The M3 decreases of the height rule under these windows come from the shorter window. The outcome is decided on the code's thirds, where all three windows have the same length. The per-trial thirds of the Fig. 6c legend (M-trial, a variant) give the same: under the prominence rule M1, M2 and M3 are above encoding (BH p 0.0006 to 0.0007) and the probe is not (0.68).

fig4hj-group-epochs¶

The increase of bursting from encoding into maintenance was driven by neurons with high mean ACG amplitude (also increasing to the probe) and neurons with a long tau decay, while the low ACG, short tau decay and concept-cell groups showed no change across epochs.

for (grule, rule, mr), _ in EPB.groupby(["grule", "rule", "mread"]):
    q = {g: epoch_tests(EPB[(EPB.group == g) & (EPB.load == 1) & (EPB.grule == grule) & (EPB.rule == rule) & (EPB.mread == mr)])[0]
         for g in ["HighACG", "LongDecay", "LowACG", "ShortDecay", "Concept"]}
    med = {g: EPB[(EPB.group == g) & (EPB.load == 1) & (EPB.grule == grule) & (EPB.rule == rule) & (EPB.mread == mr)][PER].median()
           for g in ["HighACG", "LongDecay"]}
    hi = {k: bool(q["HighACG"][f"enc-{k}"] < 0.05 and med["HighACG"][k] > med["HighACG"]["enc"]) for k in ["M1", "M2", "probe"]}
    lo = {k: bool(q["LongDecay"][f"enc-{k}"] < 0.05 and med["LongDecay"][k] > med["LongDecay"]["enc"]) for k in ["M1", "M2", "M3"]}
    none = {g: int(sum(v < 0.05 for v in q[g].values())) for g in ["LowACG", "ShortDecay", "Concept"]}
    print(f"{grule}/{rule}/M-{mr}: high ACG up at {hi}; long tau decay up at {lo}; significant pairs in low ACG, short tau decay, concept {none}")

Result: partially reproduced. With the prominence rule, the code's thirds and the code's groups, long tau decay neurons increase from encoding to M1, M2 and M3 and the low ACG, short tau decay and concept groups have no significant pair, but high ACG neurons increase at M1 and M2 and not at the probe (BH p 0.38). With the Methods' groups and thirds the low ACG and short tau decay groups have 6 and 7 significant pairs, and with the Methods' groups and the code's thirds none. The increases hold for one of the two groups. With the per-trial thirds (M-trial) and the code's groups, high ACG rise at M1 and M2 and long tau decay only at M1, and no reading makes high ACG rise to the probe.

Result: reproduced. Under the Methods' groups with the prominence rule, with the code's thirds and with the per-trial thirds, all cells, high ACG and long tau decay neurons have more bursts in each maintenance window than in encoding at loads 2 and 3, as at load 1; with the Methods' 1 s windows long tau decay does not at load 2. Under the code's groups the long tau decay group does not at loads 2 and 3; under the height rule the pattern does not hold.

Fit-dependent groups: stability, and decay groups from the shipped tau decay¶

The low and high ACG and short and long tau decay groups, and the PY and IN groups, are built from the ACG fit. The cell below rebuilds every group from each fit variant of the acg-fit-yield check, and from the main features with tau decay replaced by the code's shipped MATLAB value (Cell_metrics.xlsx, column Decay, an outside input used for comparison only), and reruns the encoding (fig4c), 2.8 s and own maintenance (fig4d, fig4-acg-group-differences) and epoch (fig4hj, ext2) analyses for the groups that change, with the real threshold, each group's seed unchanged.

In [44]:
VAR = {k: (F, TYPESV[k]) for k, F in FEATV.items() if k != "main"}
VAR["shipped tau decay"] = (FEAT["a"].assign(tau_decay=SHIP_CM["Decay"].values), TY)
GRV = {}
for vname, (F, ty) in VAR.items():
    for grule in ["code", "methods"]:
        G = wm.burst_groups(NT, F, CONCEPT, ty, grule)
        GRV[(vname, grule)] = G
        ov = {g: f"{sum(len(set(G[g].get(s, [])) & set(GR[grule][g].get(s, []))) for s in GR[grule][g])}/{sum(len(v) for v in GR[grule][g].values())}"
              for g in ["LowACG", "HighACG", "ShortDecay", "LongDecay", "PY", "IN"]}
        print(f"{vname}, {grule} groups: neurons shared with the main groups {ov}")
RCONF = [c for c in CONFIGS if c[2] == "real"]
jobs, keys = [], []
for (vname, grule), G in GRV.items():
    for g in FAM:
        if G[g] == GR[grule][g]:
            continue
        for rule, dist, thr in RCONF:
            for epoch, key, win in [("enc", "enc", 1.0), ("maint", "maint28", 2.8), ("maint_own", "maint28", 2.8)]:
                for sub, nids in G[g].items():
                    jobs.append(([EP[(n, 1, key)] for n in nids], win, wm.stable_seed(g, sub, epoch, rule, dist, thr, grule),
                                 rule, dist, thr, MDUR[sub] if epoch == "maint_own" else None))
                    keys.append(dict(variant=vname, grule=grule, rule=rule, dist=dist, thr=thr, epoch=epoch, group=g, sub=sub))
res = wm.pmap(wm.group_bursts_seeded, jobs)
NEW = pd.DataFrame([dict(**k, real=r[0], sur=r[1]) for k, r in zip(keys, res)])
print(f"{len(jobs)} group bursts rerun")


def variant_br(vname):
    """The burst table of a variant: rerun rows for the groups that change, the main rows otherwise."""
    new = NEW[NEW.variant == vname].drop(columns="variant")
    keep = BR[BR.thr == "real"].merge(new[["grule", "group"]].drop_duplicates(), how="left", indicator=True)
    return pd.concat([keep[keep._merge == "left_only"].drop(columns="_merge"), new], ignore_index=True)


def acg_four(df):
    out = {}
    for e in ["enc", "maint"]:
        x = df[df.epoch == e].pivot(index="sub", columns="group", values="real")
        for a, b in [("LowACG", "HighACG"), ("ShortDecay", "LongDecay")]:
            xx = x[[a, b]].dropna()
            out[(e, a)] = (xx[a].median(), xx[b].median(), wilcoxon(xx[b], xx[a], zero_method="wilcox").pvalue)
    return out


rows = []
for vname in ["main"] + list(VAR):
    df0 = BR[BR.thr == "real"] if vname == "main" else variant_br(vname)
    for (grule, rule, dist), df in df0.groupby(["grule", "rule", "dist"]):
        o = real_vs_null(df[df.epoch == "enc"], FAM, ())
        named, others = fig4c_rule(o)
        ok, pc = fig4d_rule(real_vs_null(df[df.epoch == "maint_own"], FAM, ()))
        r = {"variant": vname, "reading": f"{grule}/{rule}/d{dist}/real",
             "4c named": named, "4c others": ",".join(others) or "-",
             "4c LowACG q": round(float(o[o.group == "LowACG"].p_BH.iloc[0]), 4),
             "4d five": all(ok.values()), "4d fail": ",".join(k for k, v in ok.items() if not v) or "-",
             "4d concept q": round(pc, 3)}
        if dist == 2:
            a4 = acg_four(df)
            r.update({"low>high enc p": round(a4[("enc", "LowACG")][2], 4) if a4[("enc", "LowACG")][0] > a4[("enc", "LowACG")][1] else "lower",
                      "low>high maint p": round(a4[("maint", "LowACG")][2], 4) if a4[("maint", "LowACG")][0] > a4[("maint", "LowACG")][1] else "lower",
                      "short>long enc p": round(a4[("enc", "ShortDecay")][2], 4) if a4[("enc", "ShortDecay")][0] > a4[("enc", "ShortDecay")][1] else "lower",
                      "short-long maint p": round(a4[("maint", "ShortDecay")][2], 4)})
        rows.append(r)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

# Epoch analyses (fig4hj, ext2) for the variants' changed ACG and decay groups.
erows = []
for (vname, grule), G in GRV.items():
    for g in ["HighACG", "LongDecay", "LowACG", "ShortDecay"]:
        for rule in ["prominence", "height"]:
            for mr in ["methods", "code", "trial"]:
                for L in [1, 2, 3]:
                    for sub, nids in G[g].items():
                        c = wm.epoch_burst_counts({"enc": [EP[(n, L, "enc")] for n in nids],
                                                   "maint": [EP[(n, L, "maint3")] for n in nids],
                                                   "probe": [EP[(n, L, "probe")] for n in nids]}, rule, 2, mr,
                                                  mdurs=T[sub][T[sub].load == L].maint_dur.values)
                        erows.append(dict(variant=vname, grule=grule, rule=rule, mread=mr, load=L, group=g, sub=sub, **c))
EPV = pd.concat([EPB.assign(variant="main"), pd.DataFrame(erows)], ignore_index=True)
rows = []
for (vname, grule, rule, mr), x0 in EPV.groupby(["variant", "grule", "rule", "mread"], sort=False):
    q = {g: epoch_tests(x0[(x0.group == g) & (x0.load == 1)])[0] for g in ["HighACG", "LongDecay", "LowACG", "ShortDecay"]}
    med = {g: x0[(x0.group == g) & (x0.load == 1)][PER].median() for g in ["HighACG", "LongDecay"]}
    hi = [k for k in ["M1", "M2", "probe"] if q["HighACG"][f"enc-{k}"] < 0.05 and med["HighACG"][k] > med["HighACG"]["enc"]]
    lo = [k for k in ["M1", "M2", "M3"] if q["LongDecay"][f"enc-{k}"] < 0.05 and med["LongDecay"][k] > med["LongDecay"]["enc"]]
    e2 = {}
    for g in ["HighACG", "LongDecay"]:
        e2[g] = all(all(x0[(x0.group == g) & (x0.load == L)][k].median() > x0[(x0.group == g) & (x0.load == L)]["enc"].median()
                        for k in ["M1", "M2", "M3"]) for L in [1, 2, 3])
    rows.append({"variant": vname, "reading": f"{grule}/{rule}/M-{mr}", "4hj high ACG up at": ",".join(hi) or "-",
                 "4hj long decay up at": ",".join(lo) or "-",
                 "4hj sig pairs low ACG, short decay": f"{sum(v < 0.05 for v in q['LowACG'].values())}, {sum(v < 0.05 for v in q['ShortDecay'].values())}",
                 "ext2 high ACG": e2["HighACG"], "ext2 long decay": e2["LongDecay"]})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result (stability check). The fit variants change 0 to 3 neurons in each ACG, tau decay and cell-type group; the shipped tau decay changes the decay groups more (48 and 49 of 72 neurons kept in the code's short and long groups, 107 and 110 of 132 in the Methods'). fig4c: the Methods' groups with the height rule and a spacing of 1 bin give the paper's pattern under the main fit, under each of the three fit variants and with the shipped tau decay (low ACG BH p 0.0385 to 0.0483); with a spacing of 2 bins they give it under the main fit, two of the fit variants and the shipped tau decay (0.0385 to 0.0483) but not under the start point x (1 + 1e-9) (0.0601). So fig4c holds with the 1-bin spacing under every fit, and with the 2-bin spacing it depends on rounding. fig4d: with the Methods' groups and the prominence rule the five named groups exceed the null over each trial's own maintenance under every variant, and concept cells do not (BH p 0.225 and 0.345). fig4-acg-group-differences: with this attempt's tau decay, short does not exceed long in encoding under the prominence rule for any fit (p 0.06 to 0.17); with the shipped tau decay it does (p 0.0078 with the code's groups, 0.0156 with the Methods'), while low ACG exceeds high ACG in both epochs (p 0.0005) and short and long do not differ in maintenance (p 0.074 and 0.35). With the paper's own tau decay the claim's whole pattern appears, so its shortfall here may come from this attempt's fit; the shipped values are an outside input used for comparison only, and the outcome is not changed. fig4hj: under every variant high ACG never rise to the probe, and with the code's groups and thirds long tau decay rise at M1, M2 and M3 and low ACG and short tau decay have no significant pair. ext2: with the Methods' groups and the prominence rule high ACG and long tau decay exceed encoding at every load with the code's thirds and with the per-trial thirds under every variant; with the Methods' 1 s windows long tau decay fails under the main fit, the three fit variants and the shipped tau decay.

fig5kl-concept-cell-types¶

Of the classified concept cells, 11 were putative pyramidal and 14 putative interneurons; pyramidal concept cells showed pronounced bursting, interneuron concept cells smoother regular spiking.

reading (b): concept cells PY 11, IN 14, unclassified 33; Royer burst index median PY 0.949, IN 0.390; ISI CV median PY 2.690, IN 4.617; Holt CV2 median PY 1.217, IN 0.991
paper: PY 11 (9.9 to 12.1), IN 14 (12.6 to 15.4)

Result: reproduced. Under reading (b) of the types, 11 concept cells are PY and 14 IN, the paper's counts, and PY concept cells have the higher Royer burst index (median 0.949 against 0.390) and Holt CV2 (1.217 against 0.991). Under reading (a) the counts are 11 and 16, IN just above tolerance (12.6 to 15.4), with the same ordering (burst index 0.992 against 0.424, CV2 1.198 against 0.994).

fig6ab-celltype-bursts-vs-null¶

Pyramidal populations showed elevated bursting over a null in both encoding and maintenance, whereas interneurons showed elevated bursting during maintenance but not during encoding.

Null readings: (a) the Poisson surrogates of fig4c (the PY and IN rows of its tables, BH over the code's eight groups); (b) shuffling the cell-type labels among each participant's classified neurons, group sizes kept (100 shuffles), BH over the two groups.

In [46]:
CT6 = []
for types_reading, fam, names in [("a", FAM, ["PY", "IN"]), ("b", FAM_B, ["PY_b", "IN_b"])]:
    for epoch in ["enc", "maint", "maint_own"]:
        tab = BURST_ENC if epoch == "enc" else (BURST_M if epoch == "maint" else BURST_MO)
        if types_reading == "b":
            tab = show_bursts(epoch, FAM_B)
        x = tab[tab.group.isin(names)]
        CT6.append(x.assign(types=types_reading, epoch=epoch))
        print(f"(a) Poisson null, types ({types_reading}), {epoch}:")
        print(x[["reading", "group", "n", "real_median", "null_median", "real_above", "W", "p", "p_BH"]].round(4).to_string(index=False))
CT6 = pd.concat(CT6)
for (types_reading, reading), x in CT6.groupby(["types", "reading"], sort=False):
    q = {(e, g[:2]): float(x[(x.epoch == e) & (x.group.str[:2] == g[:2])].p_BH.iloc[0]) for e in ["enc", "maint", "maint_own"] for g in ["PY", "IN"]}
    above = {(e, g[:2]): bool(x[(x.epoch == e) & (x.group.str[:2] == g[:2])].real_median.iloc[0] > x[(x.epoch == e) & (x.group.str[:2] == g[:2])].null_median.iloc[0])
             for e in ["enc", "maint", "maint_own"] for g in ["PY", "IN"]}
    for me in ["maint", "maint_own"]:
        ok = (q[("enc", "PY")] < 0.05 and above[("enc", "PY")] and q[(me, "PY")] < 0.05 and above[(me, "PY")]
              and q[(me, "IN")] < 0.05 and above[(me, "IN")] and q[("enc", "IN")] >= 0.05)
        print(f"types ({types_reading}), {reading}, maintenance as {me}: paper's pattern {ok}; BH p PY enc {q[('enc', 'PY')]:.4f}, "
              f"PY maint {q[(me, 'PY')]:.4f}, IN maint {q[(me, 'IN')]:.4f}, IN enc {q[('enc', 'IN')]:.4f}")
rows = []
for types_reading in ["a", "b"]:
    ty_r = TYPES[types_reading]
    for epoch, key, win in [("enc", "enc", 1.0), ("maint", "maint28", 2.8)]:
        subs = sorted(set(NT["sub"].values[[n for n in range(len(NT)) if ty_r[n] in ("PY", "IN")]]))
        for sub in subs:
            nids = NT.nid[NT["sub"] == sub].values
            pyn = [n for n in nids if ty_r[n] == "PY"]
            inn = [n for n in nids if ty_r[n] == "IN"]
            if len(pyn) == 0 or len(inn) == 0:
                continue
            rng = np.random.default_rng(wm.stable_seed("typeshuffle", epoch, sub) if types_reading == "a" else wm.stable_seed("typeshuffle", epoch, sub, "b"))
            npy, nin = wm.type_shuffle_null([EP[(n, 1, key)] for n in pyn], [EP[(n, 1, key)] for n in inn], win, rng)
            for g, nl, members in [("PY", npy, pyn), ("IN", nin, inn)]:
                if len(members) >= 3:
                    rc, _, _, _ = wm.group_bursts([EP[(n, 1, key)] for n in members], win, rng, "prominence", 2, "real", n_sur=0)
                    rows.append({"types": types_reading, "epoch": epoch, "group": g, "sub": sub, "real": rc, "sur": nl})
SH = pd.DataFrame(rows)

Result: partially reproduced. No reading gives the paper's full pattern, with either cell types (the paper's pattern lines above). Against the Poisson null with the prominence rule, PY exceed the null in encoding (BH p 0.0044 to 0.0115) and maintenance, and IN in maintenance, but IN also exceed it in encoding (BH p 0.011 to 0.045), where the paper finds no difference. With the height rule PY do not differ from the null in encoding (BH p 0.06 to 0.67). As in fig4d, the 2.8 s maintenance window inflates the real-to-null comparison; with each trial's own maintenance PY still exceed the null in maintenance under the real threshold, and IN do under some readings (BH p 0.009 to 0.16). Against the label-shuffled null, PY exceed it in both epochs (BH p 0.0029 to 0.0057), and IN fall below it in encoding (BH p 0.0016 and 0.0020) and in maintenance do not exceed it (types a, BH p 0.063) or fall below it (types b, 0.015). Elevated PY bursting in both epochs holds; IN maintenance bursting holds against the Poisson null only.

fig6cd-celltype-epochs¶

Pyramidal burst rates stayed stable across task epochs at every load, whereas interneuron burst rates changed from encoding to each maintenance window and to the probe in load 1 trials.

Result: not reproduced. With the prominence rule and the code's thirds, PY have no pair of periods with BH p < 0.05 at any load, and IN burst more in M1, M2 and M3 than in encoding at load 1 (BH p 0.0047 to 0.014), but IN do not differ between encoding and the probe (0.80; 0.13 to 1.0 under every reading and both cell types). The criterion's partial outcome needs the whole pattern at load 1, which fails at the probe. The Methods' windows make PY differ. The IN change is an increase (medians 11 to 15). With the types of reading (b) the result is the same: under the prominence rule and the code's thirds PY have no significant pair at any load and IN rise at M1 to M3 (BH p 0.0058 to 0.0074) but not at the probe (1.0). The per-trial thirds of the Fig. 6c legend (M-trial) give the same: PY have no significant pair at any load, and IN rise at M1 to M3 (BH p 0.0073 to 0.038; types b 0.016 to 0.028) but not at the probe (0.65; types b 1.0).

Result: partially reproduced. With the types of reading (a), matched trials and the shared permutation, IN are load-modulated (13.95%, 30 of 215, p = 0.001), within tolerance, and so are IN concept cells (18.75%, 3 of 16, p = 0.042), just below the tolerance of 19.28 to 23.56%, while PY (5.88%, p = 0.43) and PY concept cells (0%, p = 1.0) are not. With the within-participant permutation IN concept cells give 18.75% too, and with all trials 25.00% (4 of 16), above the tolerance; the tie rule of fig1e does not change the IN concept count. The cell types move with rounding: two of the four fits of the stability check (the start point x (1 + 1e-9) and the ACG x (1 + 1e-12)) give 15 IN concept cells, of which 3 are load-modulated with matched trials (20.00%, p 0.032 to 0.040, with IN 13.08 to 14.15%), and meet the criterion; the main fit and the start point x (1 - 1e-9) give 16 IN concept cells and 18.75% with matched trials under every permutation and tie rule. With reading (b) of the types (14 IN concept cells, the paper's number), matched trials, 2 are significant (14.29%, p = 0.15) under either permutation; with all trials 3 are (21.43%, p = 0.032, within tolerance), but then IN give 17.68%, above tolerance (PY 9.00%, p = 0.075). The load modulation of IN and IN concept cells, and its absence in PY, hold under every fit; the IN concept percentage that the criterion tests is within tolerance under two of the four fits but not under the main one, so the claim holds in part.

fig6gh-in-concept-cv2¶

Interneuron concept cells had higher CV2 during maintenance than encoding on preferred load 1 trials but not on nonpreferred trials, while pyramidal concept cells showed stable CV2.

Holt's CV2 of the interspike intervals of each cell's spikes concatenated over preferred (or nonpreferred) trials, in encoding (first image, 1 s) and maintenance (2.5 s); trials of load 1 (Results) or of all loads (the code). Readings for PY: (a) encoding against maintenance within each trial type; (b) preferred against nonpreferred within each epoch.

In [53]:
def cv2_cell(n, loads, pref_flag, epoch, within=False):
    t = T[NT["sub"].iat[n]]
    t = t[t.load.isin(loads)]
    pm = pref_mask(t, PREF[n], 1) if loads == [1] else ((t.img1 == PREF[n]) | ((t.load >= 2) & (t.img2 == PREF[n])) | ((t.load == 3) & (t.img3 == PREF[n]))).values
    t = t[pm if pref_flag else ~pm]
    on, win = (t.enc1.values, 1.0) if epoch == "enc" else (t.maint.values, 2.5)
    sp = wm.epoch_spikes(SPK[n], on, on + win, win)
    if within:
        # only interspike intervals within a trial, pairs of consecutive intervals within a trial
        v = [2 * np.abs(np.diff(d)) / (d[1:] + d[:-1]) for d in (np.diff(x) for x in sp) if len(d) > 1]
        return float(np.mean(np.concatenate(v))) if v else np.nan
    return wm.cv2_holt(np.diff(wm.concat_trials(sp, win)))

The PY and nonpreferred parts hold (no comparison with p < 0.05). With the types of reading (b) IN preferred p = 0.67 (load 1) and 0.24 (all loads). Concatenating trials adds intervals that cross trial boundaries; counting only intervals within trials (a variant outside the criterion's method) gives IN preferred maintenance above encoding with p = 0.12 at load 1 and 0.0034 over all loads, IN nonpreferred p 0.32 to 1.0, and PY preferred against nonpreferred p 0.039 to 0.85, and PY preferred encoding against maintenance p = 0.037 over all loads.

ext5gh-py-decay-preferred¶

Pyramidal concept cells showed increased decay time constants on preferred trials during encoding and maintenance, an effect absent in interneurons.

tau_decay of the CellExplorer fit (acg-fit-yield) to the narrow ACG of each concept cell's spikes in the epoch of preferred (or nonpreferred) trials, concatenated; preferred against nonpreferred by a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over cells (a paired t-test as a variant); load 1 or all loads. The claims file takes this reading of "decay time constants" and the outcome rests on it.

In [54]:
def decay_cell(n, loads, pref_flag, epoch):
    t = T[NT["sub"].iat[n]]
    t = t[t.load.isin(loads)]
    pm = ((t.img1 == PREF[n]) | ((t.load >= 2) & (t.img2 == PREF[n])) | ((t.load == 3) & (t.img3 == PREF[n]))).values
    if loads == [1]:
        pm = (t.img1 == PREF[n]).values
    t = t[pm if pref_flag else ~pm]
    on, win = (t.enc1.values, 1.0) if epoch == "enc" else (t.maint.values, 2.5)
    s = wm.concat_trials(wm.epoch_spikes(SPK[n], on, on + win, win), win)
    if len(s) < 3:
        return np.nan, len(s)
    f = wm.fit_acg(wm.acg(np.sort(s), 0.0005, 201))
    return f["tau_decay"], len(s)


for tlab, loads, lname in [("a", [1], "load 1"), ("a", [1, 2, 3], "all loads"), ("b", [1], "load 1"), ("b", [1, 2, 3], "all loads")]:
    for ty_ in ["PY", "IN"]:
        cells = np.where(CONCEPT & (TYPES[tlab] == ty_))[0]
        for ep in ["enc", "maint"]:
            a = np.array([decay_cell(n, loads, True, ep) for n in cells])
            b = np.array([decay_cell(n, loads, False, ep) for n in cells])
            ok = np.isfinite(a[:, 0]) & np.isfinite(b[:, 0])
            w = wilcoxon(a[ok, 0], b[ok, 0])
            tt = stats.ttest_rel(a[ok, 0], b[ok, 0])
            print(f"types ({tlab}), {lname}, {ty_} concept, {ep}: n {ok.sum()} (spikes per cell, preferred median {np.median(a[:, 1]):.0f}); "
                  f"tau_decay median preferred {np.median(a[ok, 0]):.2f} ms, nonpreferred {np.median(b[ok, 0]):.2f}; "
                  f"preferred larger in {(a[ok, 0] > b[ok, 0]).sum()}; Wilcoxon W = {w.statistic:.1f}, p = {w.pvalue:.4f}; paired t p = {tt.pvalue:.4f}")
print("paper: PY preferred larger in encoding and maintenance, Pmax = 0.029; IN all P > 0.05")

Result: not reproduced. Under the reading of the claims file (ACG tau_decay on preferred and nonpreferred spikes), PY concept cells show no preferred-trial increase in either epoch (Wilcoxon p 0.13 to 0.73), and no IN comparison has p < 0.05 (smallest 0.058, all loads, maintenance). With the types of reading (b) PY p are 0.28 to 0.43. The fits use 25 to 50 spikes per cell at load 1 (medians), which makes tau_decay per trial type a weak measure. The outcome rests on the claims file's reading.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The ACG fit is a Python port of the code's MATLAB functions, with scipy's optimizer, so R2 and the time constants differ for part of the neurons and the cell-type counts differ slightly (102 or 100 PY against 92); later analyses use these types, and each claim on cell types is also shown with the types of reading (b), whose counts match the paper's; no outcome differs between the two. The scipy fit is not stable at the level of rounding: changes of 1e-9 in its start point give 315 or 316 well-fit neurons against 317 and move the types and groups of a few neurons, which explains why counts changed between runs; the fit-dependent results are rerun under each variant, and only fig6e changes (its IN concept share is within tolerance under two of the four fits). The GLM's significance rule compares slopes that are often tied exactly with a null slope, so a few neurons sit on their threshold; the results are shown with ties counted in and out. M1 to M3 are also run as the per-trial thirds of the Fig. 6c legend, a reading the claims file does not list (asked in questions/kussovska-2025.yaml); no outcome changes with it. The concept-cell bootstrap is run with fixed seeds (the code sets none); the set used shares 57 of 58 cells with the code's list. The SVM is libsvm through sklearn's wrapper on a precomputed linear kernel, checked equal to SVC(kernel='linear'). The Poisson GLM is fitted by Newton's method, checked against sklearn. Many method details the paper leaves open were run under each reading the claims file names; outcomes that rest on one of several readings say so. The dPCA analyses are in the second notebook, with the code's design and 100 splits run in parallel. The maintenance burst comparison with the Poisson null uses each trial's own maintenance, as the 2.8 s window makes burst-free trains exceed the null. Decoding p values are the code's, against label-shuffled nulls whose means (9 to 18%) are below the paper's 20% chance; the binomial test against 20% is shown beside them.

What was found about the dataset. The dandiset holds all 902 units of the paper with the paper's region counts, and the paper's code tables link to its trials exactly. The paper's description differs from the files in the number of sessions with 108 trials (six, not five), the fixation durations (up to 1.2 s and longer, not 0.9 to 1.0 s), and the image duration, which varies by session (1.0 to 2.5 s) and is not stated. One trial (subject 9) has a maintenance of 0 s and another a fixation of 31 us. The paper's RT-modulation percentages (Fig. 1f) are reproduced exactly only with the code's predictor, which pairs every neuron with subject 1's reaction times.
